content: These units are not part of the International System of Units (SI) or the centimeter-gram-second (cgs) system, but they are still accepted for use alongside SI units. The bar and its subunits are defined as follows: 1 bar is equivalent to 100 kilopascals (kPa) or 1,000,000 dynes per square centimeter (baryes). 1 decibar (dbar) is equal to 0.1 bar, which corresponds to 10 kPa or 100,000 dynes per square centimeter. 1 millibar (mbar) is equal to 0.001 bar, which is equivalent to 0.1 kPa, 1 hectopascal (hPa), or 1,000 dynes per square centimeter. (Note: A pascal (Pa) is defined as one newton per square meter.) The term bar originates from the Greek word βάρος (baros), which translates to weight. The official symbol for the bar is bar. An earlier symbol, b, is now deprecated but is still occasionally used, particularly in the abbreviation mb for millibars, instead of the more accurate mbar. The bar and millibar were introduced by Sir Napier Shaw in 1909 and were internationally adopted in 1929.25 mbar (or hPa), which is equivalent to 1.01325 bar.1 kilopascals. After the adoption of SI units, many transitioned to using hectopascals (hPa), which are numerically equivalent to millibars, allowing them to maintain the same numeric scale. For example, Canadian weather reports use kilopascals, which could also be referred to as centibars. This is denoted as barg (bar gauge) and is often written without spaces or as bar(g). For instance, if a car tire is said to be pressurized to 2.3 bar.3 bar. Specifically, an increase of 1 decibar corresponds to an increase in depth of approximately 1.019716 meters. Unicode includes a character for mb (millibar) for compatibility with older Asian encodings. There is also a Unicode character for bar.
